levels.name: Foundations
levels.goal: Fresher: shell, files and permissions, users, packages, processes, Git and basic bash. Do a defined task correctly on one server, with review.
levels.exit_test: 30 min, no notes, fresh VM: create a sudo user with key-only SSH, find the five largest files under /var, explain every field of ls -l, and revert a bad Git commit.

levels.name: Operator
levels.goal: Junior: keep services running day to day. systemd units, journald, sockets and ports, /proc, timers, SSH, disks and inodes. Given a port, find the responsible application within minutes.
levels.exit_test: 5 min per port: given only a port number, name the process, the unit that starts it, its config file and the command that shows its logs.

levels.name: Troubleshooter
levels.goal: Mid-level: own a system end to end and find the broken layer. Routing, DNS, TLS, HTTP, reverse proxies, packet capture and syscall tracing; start Kubernetes for the CKA.
levels.exit_test: 15 min: someone says 'the site is down'. Walk DNS, route, firewall, TLS, proxy and app, and name the broken layer with evidence (a capture, a log line or curl -v output).

levels.name: Platform
levels.goal: Senior: build and run the platform others deploy to. Container internals, images, Docker networking, Traefik and Dokploy, Kubernetes (CKA), CI/CD and configuration management.
levels.exit_test: One weekend: move one Apache workload into a container behind Dokploy, built by a GitLab CI pipeline that pushes to Harbor, with a written rollback you have actually tested.

levels.name: SRE
levels.goal: Senior / Lead: make reliability a property of the team. Metrics, logs and alerts, performance analysis, incident response, postmortems and change management.
levels.exit_test: Game day: a script breaks one thing in the homelab at random. You learn about it from an alert, fix it, and publish a one-page postmortem with timeline, root cause and follow-ups.

nodes.summary: The host failures that fill Ubuntu forums and postmortems, fixed from evidence: full disks and inodes, apt and dpkg locks, restart loops, SSH lockouts, OOM kills, file limits, clocks and boots that stop in emergency mode.
nodes.why: When Dokploy, Traefik or a GitLab runner misbehaves, the cause is often one layer down on the host: a full disk, an apt lock held by a timer, a unit in a restart loop or a limit nobody raised. nodes.title: Let's Encrypt and ACME in practice: HTTP-01, DNS-01, renewals
nodes.summary: Get and keep public certificates without surprises: HTTP-01 through firewalls and proxies, DNS-01 for wildcards and internal names, renewals that really reload, rate limits, CAA and the 2026 chain change.
nodes.why: An expired or wrong certificate is the most common way a working site suddenly shows a browser warning, and the Let's Encrypt forum is full of the same causes: port 80 blocked or answered by the wrong server, an AAAA record nobody serves, renewals that never reload, rate limits hit while debugging. Invalid response ... 404 → dig +short AAAA DOMAIN, then curl -6 the probe from outside
Renewed, but browsers get the old certificate → echo | openssl s_client -connect DOMAIN:443 -servername DOMAIN 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate

nodes.title: Self-hosted platform: the open-source toolbox
nodes.summary: One realistic self-hosted platform built from open-source tools: its request, deploy, log, security and backup flows and port matrix, which alternative to pick in each category, and twelve integration recipes with what breaks between the tools.
nodes.why: Most on-prem DevOps work happens at the seams between tools: a runner trusting Harbor's CA, Traefik passing the header Authentik needs, Wazuh reading Traefik's log, a backup nobody restored. A senior engineer owns the whole picture and decides which tools belong on it.
learn: The reference platform: hosts, request, deploy, metrics, log, security and backup flows, and the port matrix
Decision tables per category: PaaS, proxies, CI/CD, registries, monitoring, logging, security, secrets, SSO, backup, VPN
Integration recipes: GitLab CI → Harbor → Dokploy, forward auth, CrowdSec in Traefik, logs to Loki and Wazuh, restic to S3
Running it safely: upgrade policy, pinned versions, backups of each tool's state, exposure rules, retiring tools
practice: Build the GitLab CI → Harbor → Dokploy recipe on a lab, roll back by re-pointing the tag, then add the Prometheus recipe so every deploy is visible on a dashboard
Draw your own platform like the big picture in section 1, fill in its port matrix, and mark every port that is reachable from the internet but should not be
troubleshoot: Login callback ends in a plain 404 after adding forward auth → curl -sI "https://APP/outpost.goauthentik.io/start?rd=https://APP/" | grep -iE '^(HTTP|location)'
CrowdSec decisions exist but nothing is blocked → docker exec CROWDSEC cscli bouncers list
Deploy API returns 200 but the old version answers → curl -s https://APP/version
nodes.exit_check: Another engineer rebuilds one component of your lab platform from your runbook without calling you, and you can defend every box on your diagram: why it exists, its open ports, its backup and its upgrade path.
